claims.text: The starting CoCrFeNi alloy is a conventionally processed, single-phase, coarse-grained material.
CoCrFeNi undergoes dynamic shear-induced grain refinement during sliding.
The starting CoCrFeNi alloy has tribological performance that varies with temperature and load.
Adding a minor reactive dopant to CoCrFeNi will cause dopant segregation or migration to the sliding surface.
The dopant will trigger controlled oxidation at the wear interface.
The dopant will enhance extreme grain refinement during sliding.
Doping will produce a continuous nanograined glaze containing beneficial oxide phases and nanoprecipitates.
A nanograined glaze and nanoprecipitates can protect and stabilize a sliding interface.
At lower temperatures, extreme grain refinement in the glaze will cause inverse Hall–Petch softening.
At higher temperatures, sliding will generate a robust protective oxide or nanocrystalline glaze film.
The adaptive interface will lower interfacial shear strength.
The adaptive glaze will suppress adhesive, oxidative, and plastic-deformation wear.
Relative to undoped CoCrFeNi, the doped alloy will attain a coefficient of friction near 0.2 throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
Relative to undoped CoCrFeNi, doping will reduce wear rate by one to several orders of magnitude throughout room temperature to 800 °C.
The friction and wear benefits will persist under both low and high normal loads.
The intervention will be effective in ambient oxidizing environments up to 800 °C.
Unstable oxide formation and inadequate interface adaptation cause the baseline CoCrFeNi alloy's inconsistent friction and wear.
The intervention's effectiveness in inert or ultrahigh-vacuum environments and at loads beyond the tested range is uncertain.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis says performance will be maintained across variable environmental conditions, whereas the boundary limits the expected benefit to ambient oxidizing environments and declares inert or ultrahigh-vacuum performance uncertain.
